award.projectOutComesReport:
This project advanced the design of reconfigurable wideband transceivers and multi-band antennas to enable efficient coexistence between passive and active spectrum users. The work addressed a critical challenge in modern wireless systems: how to share crowded spectrum resources without interference, while reducing hardware complexity and cost.

Intellectual Merit
The research began with optimization tools for satellite communication arrays, demonstrating that sparse array designs could reduce hardware while maintaining gain. Building on this foundation, the team designed and fabricated a reconfigurable beam-steering antenna array at millimeter-wave frequencies, achieving wide scanning angles with high gain and bandwidth.

Machine learning was introduced into antenna design, enabling efficient optimization of compact patch antennas for CubeSat applications. Fabricated prototypes closely matched predicted and simulated results, validating AI-driven design methods. In parallel, a W-band material characterization tool was developed to extract dielectric properties of materials for high-frequency RF design.

Subsequent work produced shared-aperture multi-band antennas that integrate sub-6 GHz and millimeter-wave bands. These designs achieved strong inter-band isolation and stable broadside radiation, supporting compact and efficient integration for next-generation platforms. The effort culminated in the fabrication and validation of tri-band and quad-band shared-aperture antennas, as well as a dual-polarized aperture-in-aperture antenna for UAVs that combines GPS L1 and Ka-band satellite links in a single ultra-low-profile package. These designs demonstrated manufacturability, high gain, and compactness.

Broader Impacts

  • Technology Transfer: Two patents were granted on multi-band antenna systems, establishing intellectual property protection and creating pathways for commercialization. The compact, multi-band designs are directly relevant to UAV manufacturers, satellite communication providers, and defense contractors.
  • Training and Workforce Development: Graduate and undergraduate students gained extensive training in RF simulation, fabrication, and measurement. Students learned HFSS, vector network analyzer calibration, and multilayer PCB fabrication, preparing them for careers in RF engineering. One Ph.D. student graduated and transitioned to industry, while undergraduate trainees advanced to graduate study.
  • Dissemination: Results were presented at four major international conferences, including IEEE Antennas and Propagation, URSI Asia-Pacific Radio Science Conference, and URSI-B Electromagnetic Theory Symposium. In total, six journal papers were produced (three published, one submitted, and two in preparation), alongside the two granted patents. These outputs ensured broad visibility and impact across both academic and industry communities.
  • Public Benefit: The compact, reconfigurable antenna architectures developed here have direct applications in UAV navigation, disaster response, and resilient communication systems. By reducing hardware requirements and introducing AI-driven design, the project points toward more affordable and efficient wireless systems for both commercial and public use.

Summary
Across the life of the award, the project achieved critical milestones: optimization of sparse arrays for satellite links, fabrication of reconfigurable beam-steering arrays, validation of machine learning methods for antenna design, and development of shared-aperture multi-band systems. Altogether, the project produced six journal papers, four international conference presentations, and two patents. These accomplishments established the technical foundation for technology transfer, trained the next generation of engineers, and demonstrated clear pathways toward practical, low-cost, and high-performance wireless technologies. The final phase emphasized dissemination and commercialization, ensuring that the innovations developed under this award will continue to impact both academic research and public applications.

award.abstractText:
This project seeks to address the problem of spectrum pollution in the Internet-of-Things (IoT) era. Spectrum pollution is an inevitable challenge that emerges when low-cost and low-power wireless IoT devices deployed at scale cannot detect and respect the presence of other devices on shared spectrum. The core challenge is the low-power and simplicity of most IoT devices, due to which they are narrowband and unable to sense and avoid incumbents on shared spectrum. The project investigates a system that allows teams of geo-distributed low-power devices to quickly and efficiently scan wide bandwidths to avert interference. This proposal presents Swallow, a system design for low-power devices to sense spectrum at minimal energy and cost, allowing these devices to behave as low-cost and distributed spectrum observatories. The testbed developed through the project will serve as a vehicle for undergraduate and graduate-level projects as well as workshops for K-12 students in the City of Pittsburgh. The team has direct experience working with sensor deployments both at Carnegie Mellon, the City of Pittsburgh, United States Geological Survey (USGS), and local industry partners and will leverage these connections to deploy Swallow at scale.

The project will study a low-power analog frontend and associated digital processing that allows IoT devices to summarize large bandwidths using inexpensive components. It investigates an end-to-end system design that collates measurements from distributed individually low-power IoT devices to obtain a shared spectrum map. It further develops an accurate localization framework to geo-locate individual IoT devices to sample spectrum occupancy at fine-spatial resolution. The wide bandwidth of Swallow’s low-power frontend naturally leads to an accurate solution for time-of flight based localization, where bandwidth is a key metric that dictates system accuracy. Swallow proposes a sub-meter accurate ranging solution for low-power wide-area radios that enables detecting proximity to known passive RF devices such as fixed radio telescopes and enables spectrum occupancy maps sampled at fine-spatial resolution. The project will be implemented and evaluated on a large programmable Low-Power Wide-Area Networking testbed in the Carnegie Mellon University campus that serves large parts of the City of Pittsburgh.

In this project, we developed a variety of mechanisms using teams of geo-distributed, low-power devices capable of quickly and efficiently scanning wide bandwidths to avert interference. We developed a novel to enable low-power devices to sense the spectrum at minimal energy and cost. This design effectively transforms these devices into a network of low-cost, distributed spectrum observatories. 


The project led to the publication of RFIMap (MobiCom 2023), a system that aims to inexpensively characterize the spatial and temporal distribution of RF spectrum occupancy of any indoor space at fine granularity (tens of centimeters). RFIMap reports wide-band indoor spectrum occupancy maps using low-cost and battery-free commodity RFID tags. RFIMap’s spectrum maps have wide-ranging applications such as monitoring ambient interference in smart manufacturing, and smart hospitals. RFIMap relies on the observation that commodity RFID tags naturally reflect ambient transmission at other frequency bands, without any modification. RFIMap uses these reflections toestimate the ambient signal power originally received at these tags. RFIMap further performs a careful modeling of indoor multipath to build a dense spectrum map with fine spatial granularity.


The project also led to the publication of various sytems impacting other domains under the broad umbrella of distributed spectrum management and sensing. Vista (ToSN 2024) is a communication system that adapts encoding onboard the CubeSat and decoding configuration on commercial LoRa ground stations to allow images to be communicated in a spectrum-efficient manner. TagFi (UbiComp 2021) is a backscatter based system for localizing devices using ambient Wi-Fi signals and an ultra low-power platform. OwLL (IPSN 2021) is a LoRa localization system that limits location tracking error to a few meters with commodity LoRa clients in a wide-area network. CharIoT (IEEE TMC 2020) is the first cross-technology distributed MIMO receiver system that exploits the potential of distributed MIMO to facilitate better co-existence and decoding of a large number of simultaneous low power uplink transmissions from unmodified low-power clients. NulLoRa (SECON 23), a system that uses antenna nulling patterns at scale across a LoRaWAN network to collaboratively improve overall system capacity. 


In terms of broader impacts, the system has been deployed and evaluated at the Greenbank observatory for radio frequency inference monitoring (RFI 2024 paper). We have also extensively engaged with K-12 student populations through the CMU Gelfand center.

The goal of this 5-year Faculty Development in the Space Sciences (FDSS) project is to enable a new faculty hire in the geospace sciences at the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the West Virginia University (WVU).  The current geospace plasma science group at the WVU is  multifaceted, with five tenured/tenure-track faculty, a research professor, and a teaching professor who also is active in geospace research.  The group's expertise spans the gamut of approaches to geospace  plasma science research, including laboratory experiment, theory, high-performance computing, machine learning, solar observations, magnetospheric observations, and CubeSat development.  The group has a long history of success in the geospace sciences, including research, training and placement of undergraduate and graduate students, and cross-disciplinary activities.  The current geospace plasma science group is large enough to have the infrastructure to support an expanding group, including laboratory space, a diverse set of colleagues --- by research area, career stage, and gender --- and a suite of existing classes in fundamental plasma physics.  However, the group is also small enough where a new hire would have a significant impact, such as bridging links between existing faculty, bringing new capabilities, and transitioning a new graduate geospace physics special-topics course into a permanent course on a two-year cadence.  

This new faculty hire at the WVU would represent genuine growth to the geospace sciences community.  The WVU Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering recently expanded into geospace science research, providing opportunities for partnerships within the university community.  The strategic need of the geospace plasma science group at the WVU is for an experimental position, defined broadly to include laboratory investigations of geospace-relevant physics and/or development of instrumentation for observational platforms.  The department has the infrastructure to allow such a new hire to thrive, and it would present significant opportunities for student involvement in research and training to be future leaders in the field as is the intention of the FDSS program. 

A new faculty hire to the WVU geospace plasma science group supports the strategic hiring plan of the Department of Physics and Astronomy to continue the active pipeline of student training in the field and the development of the workforce in the geospace sciences.  Laboratory experiments, especially current and past ones at WVU, have been immensely successful in the training of undergraduate and graduate students and postdoctoral researchers.  The course creation enhances the infrastructure for education in geospace sciences.  The WVU geospace plasma science group has a long history of high activity in public outreach, so any new hire would have many opportunities to become involved.  This 5-year FDSS project supports the training of a graduate student and postdoctoral researcher, which is a key aspect of the FDSS program.  The WVU geospace plasma science group in particular, and the Department of Physics and Astronomy in general, has a demonstrated track-record of high regard for the principles of diversity, equity, and inclusivity in department life and demonstrated success in diverse hiring in the geospace sciences. The WVU has infrastructure to support new hires, including an ADVANCE office for diverse hires resulting from a previous NSF ADVANCE IT grant.  The research and EPO agenda of this 5-year FDSS project supports the Strategic Goals of the AGS Division in discovery, learning, diversity, and interdisciplinary research.

The broader impact/commercial potential of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project is to advance communications and on-board processing capabilities for small satellites or CubeSats, which is important with growing civil and commercial demand for satellite communications services.  The proposed payload module provides a number of cognitive communications functions focused on intelligent networking capabilities for CubeSat platforms and swarms. These functions enable robust, reliable global connectivity by allowing for customer CubeSats to efficiently and autonomously communicate within swarms and with other networks for applications including Earth observation, sensing, situational awareness, new space, and communications. 

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project will develop and demonstrate a flexible, comprehensive cognitive communications payload module to enhance communications functions in networking for CubeSat platforms and swarms. This project will demonstrate the technical feasibility of the proposed innovation, apply advanced and emerging on-board processing and communications technologies, and develop and integrate hardware and software to develop a prototype payload module for CubeSat applications. The prototype will perform several cognitive functions allowing for intelligent networking for CubeSat platforms and swarms: intelligent routing, network self-healing, ad-hoc networking with other available networks, and data store and forward capabilities for sparse networks and network build-up phase. Autonomous operation will improve data transmission, data packaging and routing, latency mitigation, and user-initiated services for commercial, government, and academic CubeSat operators.  This effort will focus on three key areas: 1) developing the cognitive engine architecture and software, 2) acquiring and integrating a software-defined radio and single-board computer, and 3) developing an appropriate API. The objective of this project is to prototype the cognitive communications payload module in preparation for testing, demonstration, flight qualification, and commercialization.

During Phase I, Comsat Architects demonstrated the feasibility of advanced link optimization and intelligent routing capabilities for our Comprehensive Cognitive Communications Payload Module (C3PM), an innovative module that enables autonomous communications functionality for CubeSats and constellations. To do this, we developed and implemented the foundational hardware (HW) and software (SW) assemblies for the C3PM, including algorithms that could autonomously optimize communication links and route data through a constellation. The C3PM is an advanced communication and computing system for CubeSat platforms that utilizes cognitive technologies, machine learning (ML) algorithms, and advanced, miniaturized computing and communications HW to achieve autonomous functionality and inter-satellite cooperation for CubeSats in a constellation. The initial functions the C3PM will perform are as follows: (1) intelligent routing, (2) data store and forwarding for sparse networks of constellation build-up phase, and (3) link performance optimization. Using standard HW and SW interfaces, the C3PM can integrate with a variety of SDRs and standard CubeSat buses. 

The C3PM greatly advances the CubeSat state of the art by providing commercial and government CubeSat operators with a unique, novel payload module designed to enable cognitive communications and on-board processing functions. Comsat Architects’ research indicates that though cognitive technologies are of great interest to researchers and the CubeSat industry, our product will be the first commercially available to provide comprehensive cognitive communications functions for CubeSat applications. CubeSat operators have indicated they are interested in solutions alleviating CubeSat swarms’ expensive burden on ground stations and high data latency. The C3PM’s on-board processing, intelligent routing, and link optimization functions allow data to be processed on the spacecraft itself instead of a ground station, and for that data to reach Earth through the fastest, most efficient path.

At the end of Phase I, we successfully developed the Cognitive Engine SW and acquired initial HW to establish the feasibility of the operations and key functions of the C3PM. We successfully integrated the development SBC, including a high-performance system on a chip (SOC), and SDR and installed our CE and API SW to build an engineering assembly as our initial prototype unit. After testing this assembly on the Communication Testbed, we verified that the C3PM HW and SW had successfully integrated and that the CE effectively allowed our system to operate and learn. We have established our module’s feasibility through verifying functionality of the link optimization and the routing pipeline, selection and acquisition of high-performance HW, successful development of CE SW, the development of a Radio API, and integration testing of the HW and SW in an engineering assembly.

The C3PM pushes forward the CubeSat state of the art significantly, providing much higher communications and on-board processing capabilities than are currently available for small satellites. The C3PM’s innovative Cognitive Engine enables advanced link optimization and intelligent routing for efficient node-to-node data transfer within a network with reduced latency. Comsat Architects has identified several application areas the C3PM can benefit including Earth observation, sensing, situational awareness, space Internet, and communications. Outside of commercial applications, the C3PM’s intelligent routing capabilities can benefit US national security and defense, science, and space exploration initiatives by allowing important information to reach decision makers more quickly. 

These accomplishments demonstrate that the C3PM, once developed, can perform cognitive functions which can now be developed to incorporate more advanced features. Going forward, we will build upon these accomplishments by developing other components of the CE, addressing remaining compatibility issues, and optimizing Phase I SW. Our Phase I successes have given us a framework to expand vital CE SW in Phase II. After working with our current development SBCs, we have a thorough understanding of all the interfaces and processing power necessary to develop and test a C3PM engineering prototype.

The accomplishments of our Phase I R&D effort have provided Comsat Architects with a strong framework for developing a prototype C3PM in Phase II and ultimately a product ready for market. The HW and SW acquired and built has highlighted that our module can perform the high-level link optimization and intelligent routing laid out in our R&D objectives. We will build upon this foundation in Phase II to develop a fully functioning prototype C3PM for demonstration in a relevant environment, bringing the C3PM a critical step closer toward utilizing its advanced cognitive communications capabilities on a CubeSat in orbit.

award.abstractText:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) Phase I project is to open new orbital flight regimes to CubeSat and microsatellite vehicles. Vehicles of these size classes are currently constrained by the lack of suitable propulsion options or additional regulatory burdens that most propulsion systems levy on rideshare vehicles. Most small satellites in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) would benefit from propulsion systems and all missions beyond LEO require on-board propulsion. The proposed  Reaction Control System (RCS) architecture would enable new beyond-LEO missions for small satellites and enhance the on-orbit lifetime and utility of LEO missions at lower costs.  

This Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) Phase I project ties satellite propulsion performance to the ever-increasing capabilities of small satellite Electrical and Power Systems (EPS) with a novel, miniaturized resistojet design and benign green propellant.  While other technologies (batteries, solar panels, power distribution systems) have improved satellite EPS, propulsion systems have lagged.  The use of a miniature resistojet in the RCS design allows the performance of the propulsion system to be decoupled from the chemical properties of propellant (largely fixed due to chemistry limitations), and instead links performance to improved EPS systems.  Additionally, the proposed RCS uses a novel non-gaseous pressurization system and a benign green propellant for improved safety on ridesharing satellites.

The Goose RCS team consisted of Maverick Space Systems and the CubeSat Lab at Cal Poly of San Luis Obispo, California. During the STTR period of performance, the Goose reaction control system (RCS) for small satellites was developed conceptually, designed to meet user specifications, and tested at a prototype level. The market fit for the design concept of a non-pressurized, non-hazardous, reaction control system for small satellites was also validated through customer discovery interviews that the team undertook.

As part of system development, the team developed thermodynamic models of the system as well as process diagrams, pseudocode software control algorithms, and electrical schematics. The team internally reviewed these design products through rigorous preliminary and critical design reviews, and then constructed prototype hardware and software to verify the teams’ models and designs.

This prototype hardware was manufactured and tested at the piece-part level and then integrated into a complete unit for hot-fire testing. Hot-fire testing was successfully completed in a simulated space environment, further validating the system models and design. This prototype proved out the pressure cycle of the system and pointed to areas where the design could be improved.

The team also designed a second prototype system which closely resembles a flight unit. The primary purpose of this prototype article was to pathfind manufacturing and allow demonstrations of additional hardware and software features not present in the first prototype.

The Goose RCS team accomplished significant advancements in the Phase I effort which they believe will begin to enable the Small Satellite and New Space communities to utilize this propulsion system on a broader scale, while also serving the science, education, and military communities and their in-space technological abilities.

award.abstractText:
The jointly funded NSF/NASA ELFIN mission consists of two identical CubeSats on a polar (~ 93 degree inclination), nearly circular, low-Earth orbit. ELFIN was launched on September 15, 2018 and is currently operating within the geospace environment. This funding will address the prime mission objective of analyzing the data currently being collected by ELFIN to advance understanding of wave-particle interactions and their effect on relativistic electrons in the outer radiation belt. Two undergraduate students, a graduate student, and three early career scientists will be supported. ELFIN data products are integrated into courses at UCLA and in public outreach events in the Los Angeles area.

The project will utilize ELFIN, together with its conjunctions with other, equatorial Heliophysics missions to address the efficacy of EMIC wave precipitation, and the relative contribution of EMIC, whistlers and kinetic Alfvén waves in the observed relativistic electron scattering (100s of keV to a few MeV energy). The specific science objectives are: (1) Are EMIC waves responsible for 0.5-2MeV electron precipitation?
(2) Are waves other than EMIC waves (principally chorus waves and kinetic Alfvén waves (KAWs)), also responsible for significant relativistic electron scattering? (3) What are the typical precipitation rates associated with various wave types as function of geomagnetic conditions?

award.projectOutComesReport:
ELFIN has explored the relative role and significance of EMIC wave scattering for relativistic electron precipitation. Relativistic electron loss from the outer radiation belt occurs by EMIC waves, Field-Line-Curvature scattering and ducted chorus waves primarily at dawn and secondarily at premidnight. The primary means of sub-relativistic electron loss and energy deposition appears to be whistler-mode waves of various types. Sub-relativistic precipitation dominates the total energy delivered to the atmosphere by energetic particles, thus whistler-mode chorus dominate the energy deposition. The energy delivered to the atmosphere from energetic electrons under all geomagnetic conditions is only 2% of the energy by <30keV electrons. However, that energy is deposited in the mesosphere where low energies cannot reach, and therefore contributes readily to the production of NOx in winter seasons and its subsequent transport to the stratosphere by vertical winds where it can cause ozone depletion and have global atmospheric effects. Therefore, the input spectrum produced by ELFIN needs to be included in future global circulation models.

Students led science operations software development, improvements on attitude determination and higher-fidelity product generation. In all, approximately 20 undergraduate students were trained this past period (partly funded by NSF and partly by NASA/ELFIN). Graduate students continued to excel in their data analysis and interpretation of ELFIN data. Undergraduate student Ms. A. Roosnovo published a JGR paper in 2024. Graduate students, Mr. Tsai, Mr. Wilkins and Ms. Shi presented quarterly to the UCLA space physics groups. They presented talks or posters at the AGU meetings in 2021, 2022, 2023 and at the GEM meetings in the same years and published or submitted papers to JGR (Shi et al., 2022, Tsai et al., 2023, 2024 and Wilkins et al., 2023).

There have been approximately a dozen presentations on ELFIN each year in the last 4 years at GEM meetings, at COSPAR and at IUGG. Numerous invited ELFIN talks were given at these meetings, several by early career scientists such as Dr. X. -J. Zhang, and Dr. Ethan Tsai. We have continued to give tours of ELFIN and public speeches at events or gatherings, including visits from high-school students and the general public.

award.title: Collaborative Research:  Causes and Consequences of Relativistic Electron Precipitation as Revealed by the CubeSat Mission ELFIN’s Pitch-Angle Resolved Loss Cone Measurements

award.abstractText:
The jointly funded NSF/NASA ELFIN mission consists of two identical CubeSats on a polar (~ 93 degree inclination), nearly circular, low-Earth orbit. ELFIN was launched on September 15, 2018 and is currently operating within the geospace environment. This funding will address the prime mission objective of analyzing the data currently being collected by ELFIN to advance understanding of wave-particle interactions and their effect on relativistic electrons in the outer radiation belt. Two undergraduate students, a graduate student, and three early career scientists will be supported. ELFIN data products are integrated into courses at UCLA and in public outreach events in the Los Angeles area.

The project will utilize ELFIN, together with its conjunctions with other, equatorial Heliophysics missions to address the efficacy of EMIC wave precipitation, and the relative contribution of EMIC, whistlers and kinetic Alfvén waves in the observed relativistic electron scattering (100s of keV to a few MeV energy). The specific science objectives are: (1) Are EMIC waves responsible for 0.5-2MeV electron precipitation?
(2) Are waves other than EMIC waves (principally chorus waves and kinetic Alfvén waves (KAWs)), also responsible for significant relativistic electron scattering? (3) What are the typical precipitation rates associated with various wave types as function of geomagnetic conditions?

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Intellectual Merit

The ELFIN mission, consisting of two identical CubeSats in a low-Earth orbit, operated from 2018 to 2022. This collaborative project addressed the primary mission objectives through the analysis of the ELFIN CubeSat data. Electron precipitation into the upper atmosphere is a significant loss process for energetic electrons in the Earth’s inner magnetosphere. The project advanced our understanding of the effects of wave-particle interactions on energetic electron precipitation and the evolution of energetic electron fluxes in Earth's outer radiation belt. Our findings regarding the relative roles of various magnetospheric waves in energetic electron precipitation are particularly significant, as electron precipitation serves as an important energy input source, enhances ionization, induces chemical changes in the upper atmosphere, and plays a critical role in regulating ring current and radiation belt electron dynamics. The technique of analyzing the physical relationship between wave properties and wave-driven electron pitch angle scattering loss for multiple conjunction events involving near-equatorial spacecraft and the ELFIN CubeSats provided excellent opportunities to reveal the underlying physics of wave-driven electron precipitation. Furthermore, our findings contribute key insights to enhance future modeling of the roles of various magnetospheric waves in radiation belt and ring current electron dynamics, as well as energy inputs into the upper atmosphere driven by wave-induced particle precipitation.

 

Broader Impacts

Space weather poses one of the most significant threats to our increasingly technological society, given our growing dependence on space assets for navigation, communications, commerce, and finance. Our results have greatly enhanced the understanding of space weather by providing a more accurate quantification of energetic electron precipitation. This collaborative project, led by an early-career female faculty member (Prof. Wen Li at Boston University), provided hands-on training for two early-career scientists, Dr. Capannolo and Dr. Qin, who actively engaged in the ELFIN data analysis of electron precipitation. Both female postdocs were successfully promoted to research scientists during the project period. The scientific outcomes of this project have been widely disseminated through 19 peer-reviewed publications in top-rated journals and around 67 conference presentations. Additionally, Prof. Li has integrated the findings from this project into a course for space and plasma physics majors, reaching approximately 20 students, as well as into her core and advanced courses for graduate students, totaling around 30 students at Boston University.

 

Specifically, this project led to the following major outcomes.

1) Identified the causes of modulated electron precipitation: We investigated what causes electron precipitation during a specific event where modulated electron precipitation was observed at low altitudes by the ELFIN spacecraft. We found that electron precipitation occurred at energy levels from about 50 keV to less than 1 MeV and varied in intensity across different locations. Our findings show that the modulated energetic electron precipitation is influenced by hiss, plume hiss, and chorus waves.

2) Quantified the role of very oblique chorus in electron precipitation. We examined a specific event where bursts of energetic electrons, with energies between 50 and 800 keV, were observed by the twin ELFIN CubeSats. During this event, intense, very oblique whistler-mode waves were detected by the THEMIS-E satellite at the corresponding magnetic equator. Our simulations showed that the electron precipitation—especially for electrons with energies above 100 keV—was mainly caused by high-order resonant scattering from these very oblique whistler-mode waves.

3) Assessed the impact of EMIC-driven electron precipitation on the atmosphere. By combining unique electron measurements from the ELFIN CubeSats with a detailed ionization model called Boulder Electron Radiation to Ionization (BERI), we evaluated the impact of EMIC-driven electron precipitation on our atmosphere. We measured how much energy this precipitation adds to the atmosphere, pinpointed its location, and calculated the expected range of ion and electron production rates. Notably, we found that this activity peaks in the mesosphere, a layer of the atmosphere that has often been overlooked in previous studies.

4) Created a list of EMIC-driven electron precipitation events: We compiled a list of EMIC-driven electron precipitation events based on observations from the ELFIN CubeSats. We also used data from Polar Orbiting Environmental Satellites (POES) to look for nearby proton precipitation events at energies between 10s and 100s of keV, which serve as indicators of EMIC wave activity. 

5) Constructed a statistical distribution of electron precipitation: We analyzed the global distribution of electron precipitation at Low-Earth Orbit using the ELFIN data. Our findings show that during active conditions, the ratio of ~63 keV electron precipitation is highest at L-shells greater than 6, particularly at midnight. For ~1 MeV electron precipitation, the highest ratios also occur near midnight at locations greater than 6, but there is a notable increase near dusk during active periods. We observed variations in the energy levels of the precipitation, indicating how energy disperses depending on the magnetic shell location, which aligns with our understanding of how hiss waves and current sheet scattering drive these precipitation events.
